cybersecurity_questions.question: An email signed by the CEO asks you to urgently buy gift cards for a client and send the codes. What do you do?
options: A) Buy them, the sender address is correct
B) Reply to the email to confirm it first
C) Call the CEO on a number you know
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: The sender name and even the address can be faked, and a reply goes straight to the attacker. Verify unusual requests through a contact you already know.

cybersecurity_questions.question: You step away from your desk for two minutes. What do you do with your computer?
options: A) Lock it (Win + L)
B) Turn off the monitor
C) Close the open documents
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: A dark monitor or closed documents stop nobody - a few seconds at an unlocked computer are enough. Win + L takes one second.

cybersecurity_questions.question: In the car park you find a USB stick labelled "Salaries 2026". What do you do?
options: A) Plug it into a spare PC to find the owner
B) Hand it to IT without plugging it in
C) Scan it with antivirus first, then open it
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: A tempting label is bait. A USB stick can pretend to be a keyboard and run commands the moment it is plugged in, before antivirus even reacts.

cybersecurity_questions.question: Which of these passwords is the hardest to crack?
options: A) tractor-violin-cloud-mustard
B) P@ssw0rd2026!
C) Xk9#q!Lm
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: Length beats complexity. Swapping letters for @ or 0 is the first thing cracking tools try, and 8 characters are too few.

cybersecurity_questions.question: Someone from "IT support" calls and needs your password to fix your account. What do you do?
options: A) Tell them, IT needs it for the fix
B) Tell them and change it right afterwards
C) Refuse and report the call to IT
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: Real IT never needs your password - they can reset it. Changing it afterwards is too late: an attacker needs only minutes.

cybersecurity_questions.question: Which sign most reliably gives away a phishing email?
options: A) It pushes you to log in or pay via a link
B) It is full of spelling and grammar mistakes
C) It comes from an unknown sender
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: Today's phishing is often flawless and can come from a known but hacked address. The real warning sign is the request: click, log in, pay - and fast.

cybersecurity_questions.question: You get an email that looks suspicious. What is the best thing to do?
options: A) Delete it so nobody clicks on it
B) Report it to IT or the security team
C) Forward it to colleagues as a warning
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: A report lets IT block the message for everyone. Forwarding it spreads the dangerous link even further.

cybersecurity_questions.question: A pop-up on a news website says your browser is outdated and offers a download. What do you do?
options: A) Download it, updates are important
B) Download it, then scan it with antivirus
C) Close it, updates don't come from websites
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: Fake update pop-ups are a common way to spread malware. Real updates come from the system, the browser itself or IT - never from a web page.

cybersecurity_questions.question: A person in a courier vest carrying a parcel asks you to let them through the office door. What do you do?
options: A) Send them to reception
B) Let them in, they are clearly a courier
C) Let them in but walk with them
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: A vest and a parcel are the easiest disguise there is. Every visitor goes through reception, however they look.

cybersecurity_questions.question: What is the main benefit of two-factor authentication (2FA)?
options: A) You no longer need a strong, unique password
B) A stolen password alone won't log anyone in
C) It also protects the computer from viruses
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: 2FA adds a step a thief does not have, such as a code from your phone. You still need a strong password, and 2FA does not stop malware.

cybersecurity_questions.question: Which address do you use at Notino to report security issues and suspicious emails?
options: A) notino.security@gmail.com
B) security@notino-help.com
C) security@notino.com
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: Report anything suspicious to security@notino.com. Addresses on other domains, such as gmail.com or notino-help.com, do not belong to Notino.

cybersecurity_questions.question: Your bank's website is mybank.com. Which link really leads to it?
options: A) https://mybank.com.secure-login.net/
B) https://mybank-com.net/login
C) https://secure.mybank.com/login
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: What counts is the end of the domain, right before the first single slash. The first link belongs to secure-login.net, the second to mybank-com.net.

cybersecurity_questions.question: A link in an email reads www.notino.com. How do you safely check where it really leads?
options: A) Hover over it and read the real address
B) The link text shows the address, that is enough
C) Open it in a private browser window
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: Link text and destination can differ. Hovering (or a long press on a phone) shows the real address; a private window does not protect you.

cybersecurity_questions.question: A colleague writes from a new Teams account: "I lost my phone, send me the code that just came to you by SMS." What do you do?
options: A) Send it, I know the colleague's name and photo
B) Keep it and call them on a known number
C) Send it, then change my password right away
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: The code is the key to your account - most likely someone is logging in as you right now. Nobody legitimate ever needs your code.

cybersecurity_questions.question: A long-standing supplier emails that their bank account has changed and asks you to pay the next invoice to the new one. What do you do?
options: A) Confirm it by phone on a number from the contract
B) Pay to the new account, the email address is theirs
C) Ask them to confirm it by replying to the email
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: Fake bank detail changes (BEC) cost companies millions. The supplier's mailbox may be hacked, so confirm only through a contact you already had.

cybersecurity_questions.question: A service you used years ago reports a data leak. You had the same password at work. What now?
options: A) Change the password on the leaked service only
B) Nothing, I no longer use that account
C) Change it everywhere I use it, work included
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: Attackers automatically try leaked passwords on other services. Every account with the same password is at risk, not just the leaked one.

cybersecurity_questions.question: You need to quickly translate an internal contract. Which tool may you use?
options: A) Any free online translator
B) Only a tool approved by the company
C) A popular AI chat, if I delete the chat after
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: Free online tools and AI chats often keep what you paste and may train on it. Deleting the chat does not delete the data on their servers.

cybersecurity_questions.question: Where is it safest to keep your work passwords?
options: A) In an approved password manager
B) In a password-protected Excel file
C) Saved in the browser on a shared PC
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: A password manager encrypts passwords and creates unique ones. Excel protection is easy to break and a shared computer is used by others too.

cybersecurity_questions.question: You need to send a customer list to an external partner. What is right?
options: A) Email the whole list, the partner signed a contract
B) Upload it to my personal cloud and share the link
C) Send only the needed data via an approved channel
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: Share only the data the partner really needs, and only through approved channels. A personal cloud is outside company control and the data may stay there for good.

cybersecurity_questions.question: An SMS from "DPD" says delivery failed - reschedule at dpd-redelivery.com. You are expecting a parcel. What do you do?
options: A) Use the link, I am expecting a parcel
B) Check it in the courier's official app
C) Reply STOP to the SMS to be safe
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: Scammers send these to thousands of people - someone is always expecting a parcel. Track deliveries only through the app or site you open yourself.

cybersecurity_questions.question: At 11 pm your phone shows a login approval request you did not trigger. Then another one. What do you do?
options: A) Deny, change my password and report it
B) Approve it, it is probably just a glitch
C) Deny it each time, it will stop by itself
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: Someone already has your password and hopes you will approve out of fatigue. Denying is not enough - change the password and report it.

cybersecurity_questions.question: A website shows a padlock (HTTPS) in the address bar. What does it guarantee?
options: A) That the website is genuine and safe
B) Only that the connection is encrypted
C) That the site was checked for viruses
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: Phishing sites get HTTPS certificates for free too. The padlock only means nobody can read the traffic on the way - not who you are talking to.

cybersecurity_questions.question: What does the HSTS header protect against?
options: A) SQL injection in web forms
B) Password brute-forcing on the login page
C) Downgrading the connection to plain HTTP
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: HSTS tells the browser to open the site only over HTTPS, so an attacker in the middle cannot quietly switch you to unencrypted HTTP (SSL stripping).

cybersecurity_questions.question: A vulnerability has a CVSS score of 9.8. What does that tell you?
options: A) It is critical and should be patched urgently
B) It is already being actively exploited by attackers
C) A patch for it is already available from the vendor
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: CVSS rates severity from 0 to 10; 9.0 and above is critical. It does not say whether a patch exists or whether attackers already use it - that is tracked separately.

cybersecurity_questions.question: Which measure reliably prevents SQL injection?
options: A) Hiding database error messages
B) Parameterized queries
C) Encrypting the whole database
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: With parameterized queries (prepared statements) the input is always treated as data, never as part of the SQL command. Hiding errors does not stop the attack, it only hides it.

cybersecurity_questions.question: What does a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability let an attacker do?
options: A) Read any file straight from the server's disk
B) Take over the database server's system
C) Run their JavaScript in other users' browsers
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: XSS slips the attacker's script into a page other people view, where it can steal their session or act on their behalf. Defences: escaping output and a Content Security Policy.

cybersecurity_questions.question: Why is a unique salt added to each password before hashing?
options: A) So identical passwords get different hashes
B) So the password can be decrypted if needed
C) So that verifying the password is faster
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: Thanks to the salt, two users with the same password get different hashes, and precomputed rainbow tables become useless.

cybersecurity_questions.question: Which algorithm is suitable for storing user passwords?
options: A) SHA-256 with a salt
B) Argon2 or bcrypt
C) MD5 with a salt
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: SHA-256 and MD5 are fast, so attackers try billions of guesses per second even with a salt. Argon2 and bcrypt are deliberately slow, which makes guessing very expensive.

cybersecurity_questions.question: What does a DMARC record do for a company's email domain?
options: A) Encrypts emails sent between mail servers
B) Scans email attachments for malware
C) Says what to do with mail failing SPF/DKIM
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: DMARC builds on SPF and DKIM: the domain owner says whether forged mail should be rejected or quarantined, and receives reports about it.

cybersecurity_questions.question: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule say?
options: A) Back up 3 times a day, keep 2 weeks, test 1 a month
B) 3 copies of data, on 2 media types, 1 off-site
C) 3 servers, in 2 data centres, 1 copy in the cloud
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: Three copies of the data, on two different types of media, one of them off-site - ideally offline. Then at least one copy survives even ransomware.

cybersecurity_questions.question: What is a pass-the-hash attack?
options: A) Using a stolen hash itself to log in
B) Cracking a hash by trying every possible password
C) Sending a malicious hash in a phishing email
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: In Windows networks (NTLM) the hash itself works as proof of identity, so an attacker can log in with it without ever cracking it.

cybersecurity_questions.question: The 2020 SolarWinds Orion attack is a typical example of what?
options: A) A DDoS attack that took down a cloud provider
B) Ransomware spreading through email
C) A supply chain attack via a software update
cybersecurity_questions.explanation: Attackers planted malicious code into an official Orion update, which thousands of customers installed themselves. Through the supplier they reached its customers without breaking in directly.
